title: The Localization of Lesions Causing Coma
subtitle: Use respiration, pupils, eye movements and limb posture to place the level of dysfunction in a patient with depressed alertness

points.text: In humans the ARAS sits in the paramedian tegmentum of the posterior pons and midbrain.
points.quote: In humans, the ARAS lies in the paramedian tegmental region of the posterior portion of pons and midbrain

points.text: The ARAS runs from the upper pons through the midbrain to the posterior hypothalamus and thalamic reticular formation.
points.quote: extends from the superior half of the pons through the midbrain to the posterior portion of the hypothalamus and to the thalamic reticular formation

points.text: Because the MLF and the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei lie among the ARAS neurons, a brainstem cause of unresponsiveness also disturbs eye movements, and the pattern of ocular motility helps place the lesion.
points.quote: Thus, when unresponsiveness is caused by brainstem damage, the lesion affects the mechanisms of ocular motility as well

points.text: Bilateral hemispheric lesions can cause transient coma, especially with mesial frontal involvement.
points.quote: Bilateral cerebral hemispheric lesions may cause transient coma, particularly when they involve the mesial frontal region

points.text: Bilateral lesions of the anterior cingulate regions, the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation, the pallidum or the hypothalamus cause akinetic mutism.
points.quote: Lesions that cause akinetic mutism bilaterally affect the frontal region (anterior cingulate gyri), the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation, the globus pallidus, or the hypothalamus

points.text: Locked-in syndrome interrupts the descending motor pathways in the basis pontis on both sides while the dorsal reticular formation is spared, so alertness is preserved.
points.quote: These lesions involve the descending motor pathways bilaterally in the basis pontis but spare the more dorsal reticular formation

points.text: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is most often linked to bilateral thalamic dysfunction and to lesions of descending pathways from the hemispheres down to the upper pons.
points.quote: bilateral thalamic dysfunction and has also been described with lesions of the descending pathways anywhere from the cerebral hemispheres to the level of the upper pons

points.text: Apneustic breathing localizes to the lateral tegmentum of the lower pons.
points.quote: This abnormality appears with lesions of the lateral tegmentum of the lower half of the pons

points.text: Cluster breathing points to the low pons or high medulla.
points.quote: Breathing with a cluster of breaths following each other in an irregular sequence may result from low pontine or high medullary lesions

points.text: Ataxic breathing signals impending respiratory failure from dorsomedial medullary damage.
points.quote: heralds complete respiratory failure and follows damage of the dorsomedial medulla

localizationRules.rule: Pontine gaze palsy cannot be overcome
localizationRules.explanation: A lower pontine tegmental lesion makes the eyes look toward the hemiparetic side; unlike hemispheric deviation, oculocephalic or caloric stimulation does not move the eyes across.
localizationRules.quote: cause a horizontal gaze palsy toward the side of the lesion so that the eyes look toward the hemiparetic side

localizationRules.rule: Isolated failure of adduction means MLF
localizationRules.explanation: With normal pupils and normal vertical movements, think MLF in the upper pons ipsilateral to the eye that does not adduct.
localizationRules.quote: indicates a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the upper pons ipsilateral to the eye that fails to adduct

localizationRules.rule: An abnormal light reflex is structural until proven otherwise
localizationRules.explanation: The pupillary light reflex survives metabolic dysfunction, so an abnormal reflex, especially a unilateral one, points to the midbrain or the oculomotor nerve (with the drug exceptions the book lists).
localizationRules.quote: Abnormalities of this reflex, particularly when unilateral, indicate structural lesions of the midbrain or oculomotor nerve

localizationRules.explanation: Diencephalic dysfunction gives small reactive pupils, midbrain tegmental lesions give midsized fixed pupils, and pontine tegmental lesions give small pupils from interrupted sympathetic pathways.
localizationRules.quote: Pontine tegmental lesions cause small pupils due to interruption of descending sympathetic pathways

localizationRules.rule: Asymmetry argues against a metabolic cause
localizationRules.explanation: Focal motor asymmetry in a comatose patient suggests a structural lesion rather than metabolic encephalopathy.
localizationRules.quote: Asymmetric motor findings speak against the diagnosis of metabolic encephalopathy

keySyndromes.name: Akinetic mutism
keySyndromes.triad: Seemingly awake, silent and motionless + Eyes dart toward moving objects + Frontal release signs such as grasp or sucking reflex
keySyndromes.clue: Few signs of damaged descending motor pathways; frontal release or corticospinal signs favor akinetic mutism over catatonia, and the EEG may show slow waves whereas it is normal in catatonia.
keySyndromes.quote: refers to a state in which the patient, although seemingly awake, remains silent and motionless

keySyndromes.name: Locked-in syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Mute and motionless + Awake, alert and aware of self + Impaired horizontal eye movements with vertical eye and eyelid movements preserved
keySyndromes.clue: Usually basilar artery thrombosis with ventral pontine infarction; with mesencephalic lesions there are bilateral ptosis and vertical as well as horizontal ophthalmoplegia.
keySyndromes.quote: is mute and motionless (deefferented) but remains awake, alert, aware of self, and capable of perceiving sensory stimuli

keySyndromes.name: Lateral (uncal) transtentorial herniation
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral pupil dilated and sluggish + Posterior cerebral artery occlusion with hemorrhagic mesial occipital infarct + Kernohan notch hemiparesis ipsilateral to the original lesion
keySyndromes.clue: The pupil is affected first because the third nerve is compressed; later Duret hemorrhages of the midbrain tegmentum make recovery almost impossible.
keySyndromes.quote: the ipsilateral pupil becomes progressively dilated and responds sluggishly to light

keySyndromes.name: Central transtentorial herniation
keySyndromes.triad: Early diencephalic: somnolence with tiny reactive pupils + Late diencephalic: Cheyne-Stokes breathing and decorticate posturing + Midbrain-upper pons: midsized unequal pupils and decerebrate posturing + Lower pons: no eye movements + Medullary: ataxic breathing then apnea
keySyndromes.clue: All structures at one brainstem level tend to fail together, unlike compressive posterior fossa lesions.
keySyndromes.quote: the clinical picture reflects an orderly rostrocaudal progression of brainstem

keySyndromes.name: Ocular bobbing
keySyndromes.triad: Brisk bilateral downward eye movement + Slow return to midposition
keySyndromes.clue: Typical bobbing with preserved horizontal eye movements is specific but not pathognomonic of acute pontine injury; pretectal pseudobobbing has a V pattern and pretectal signs (acute hydrocephalus).
keySyndromes.quote: Ocular bobbing refers to intermittent, often conjugate, brisk, bilateral downward movement of the eyes with slow return to midposition

keySyndromes.name: Posterior fossa compression (cerebellar hemorrhage)
keySyndromes.clue: Unless massive, these lesions affect one brainstem level more than others, often asymmetrically, giving mainly unilateral brainstem and cerebellar signs.
keySyndromes.quote: Early in the clinical course, occipital headache, vomiting, and ataxia are usually prominent

boardTraps.text: Decorticate and decerebrate posturing are often produced by metabolic disorders, so they do not carry the structural implications suggested by their names.
boardTraps.quote: do not have the structural implications that their names, coined during experimental work, would suggest

boardTraps.text: Kernohan notch makes the hemiparesis ipsilateral to the mass; with a dilated pupil and ipsilateral hemiparesis, the lesion is on the side of the abnormal pupil.
boardTraps.quote: Therefore, when a dilated pupil and hemiparesis appear ipsilaterally, the original lesion is likely to be on the side of the abnormal pupil

boardTraps.text: Wrong-way eyes: thalamic (rarely basal ganglionic) lesions, almost always hemorrhagic, can drive the eyes away from the lesion, contrary to the usual rule that the eyes look toward a hemispheric lesion.
boardTraps.quote: Thalamic and, rarely, basal ganglionic lesions, almost always hemorrhagic, may produce forced deviation of the eyes to the side contralateral to the lesion

boardTraps.text: Metabolic disease can mimic the respiratory patterns of structural lesions, so check metabolic status before localizing by breathing pattern.
boardTraps.quote: caution and a thorough evaluation of the metabolic status of the patient must guide the interpretation of respiratory changes

boardTraps.text: Raised intracranial pressure from a supratentorial lesion can falsely suggest a posterior fossa lesion.
boardTraps.quote: Sixth nerve palsy and papilledema are the commonest false localizing signs

boardTraps.text: Fixed pupils do not by themselves prove irreversible coma in acute neurosurgical lesions.
boardTraps.quote: With acute neurosurgical lesions, fixed pupils are not necessarily a sign of irreversible coma
